soundField.caption: Explore how the Persian Sound Field (Bastar-e Ṣowtī) spans multiple pitch registers (Mantaqeh-ye Ṣowtī) from the lowest note of the Oud to the highest note of the Santūr, while the Potential Scale collapses all pitch classes into a single octave.

registers.label: Oud Low Register (Bam)
registers.note: Marks the lower boundary of the traditional Persian sound field (bastar-e ṣowtī).

registers.label: Tār — 6th String (Lower Register)
registers.note: Lower instrumental register on the tār, sounding an octave below the first string.

registers.label: Tār — 1st String (Middle Register)
registers.note: Primary melodic register of the tār and setār; forms the standard reference octave for the Potential Scale.

registers.label: Santūr High Register (Zīr)
registers.note: Approaches the upper boundary of the Persian sound field (highest notes of the santūr).

scaleComparison.caption: Hear the difference between the unfiltered Potential Scale, a consonant 7-note Actual Scale (two dāngs + ṭanīnī), an invalid 7-note counterexample, and a 5-note Pentatonic scale.

scales.title: Potential Scale (Gām-e Bel-Qovveh — C4 to C5)
scales.description: Contains every microtonal pitch available in one octave (including Vazīrī's D♭ and F♯). Playing all of them in one melody sounds cluttered and unmusical.

scales.title: Valid Actual Scale (Gām-e Bel-Fe'l — Heptatonic)
scales.description: A consonant 7-note selection (C–D–E–F–G–A–B♭–C) structured as two dāngs plus a ṭanīnī. Every note here can be used coherently in a piece.

scales.title: Invalid 7-Note Selection (Counterexample)
scales.description: An arbitrary pick (C, D-koron, E-koron, E♮, F, B) breaks Persian melodic consonance rules, creating awkward microtonal clusters and harsh leaps.

scales.title: Pentatonic Scale (5-Note Comparison)
scales.description: Five pitches per octave (C–D–E–G–A–C) with no semitones—common in East Asian, African, and Indigenous American traditions.

maqamBuilder.caption: All three examples use the exact same Actual Scale (C–D–E–F–G–A–B♭–C), yet changing the active dāng, degree hierarchy, and melodic model (sarmashq) produces a completely different modal ethos.

presets.label: Focus on G (5th), Resolve on D (2nd)
presets.note: Dwelling on degree 5 (G) and concluding on degree 2 (D) establishes a clear degree hierarchy and modal ethos.

presets.label: Single Lower Dāng (C–D–E–F)
presets.note: Confining the melody to a single 4-note dāng (C–D–E–F) with emphasis on E and cadence on C illustrates how a Persian mode can operate within just four pitches.

presets.label: Upper Dāng (G–A–B♭–C5) + Sarmashq
presets.note: Using the upper tetrachord (G–A–B♭–C5) with a recurring melodic turn around A and B♭ creates a bright, elevated modal character.
